utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al., Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] I'll repeat what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise. The microphone was on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll repeat what I was saying. There was a channel that was not the appropriate one. Today on Wednesday, I would like to greet everyone present, the accused, the Defence team, the Prosecution as well. I would also like to greet the registrar and the usher. We'll continue our hearing with cross-examination, and I will now give the floor to the OTP for the beginning of their cross-examination. Nevertheless, I would like to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Batinic. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, I give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to the Trial Chamber, to everyone in and around the courtroom, and to Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My name is Hedvig Moe. I'm a trial attorney with the Prosecution, and I will now be asking you some questions. I'd like to ask you a couple of general -- more general questions starting out, Witness. You said that you were born and raised in Gornji Vakuf, as far as I can remember, but then you went away for a few years to study to become an electrical engineer. How long did you stay away from Gornji Vakuf for your studies?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Gornji Vakuf 19 -- in 1974. I enrolled at university in Zagreb, the faculty for traffic. I was at that transport faculty for three years, and after a certain while, because of certain problems, I had to leave that university. I then found a job. I worked. I got married there. I served in the Yugoslav army for one year in Krusevac. I returned from the army. I continued to work. I enrolled to study mechanical engineering, and in 1977 I finally graduated from the faculty of mechanical engineering. I returned to Gornji Vakuf in 1998, so I lived and worked for a total of 14 years outside of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And am I understanding you correctly that after 1998 up until the present date you have been in Gornji Vakuf and lived there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1988.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So 1988 is when you came back, and from then on you stayed in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but Gornji Vakuf is now Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: A couple of questions to the population of Gornji Vakuf. You've touched upon the census of 1991. Would it be correct to say that there were approximately 25.000 persons living in Gornji Vakuf at the time in 1991 according to the census?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be more precise, 25.181 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And would it also be correct to say that there was a slight Muslim majority in that population?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an insignificant majority, as there were 14.063 inhabitants who declared themselves to be Muslims in the 1991 census. In percentages, that would amount to 56.1 per cent of the population. That percentage declared themselves to be Muslims. 10.706 inhabitants said they were Croats or, rather, 43.6 per cent of the population. 1.3 per cent, the remainder, were Serbs, of whom there were about a hundred and ten, and Yugoslavs, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you for those specifications. And also, if I understood you correctly, there was a -- and that would be slight, a slight Muslim majority, also, in the Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, if we go back to 1992, and the War Presidency later on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The composition of the Assembly after the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina was as follows: 26 Muslims and 24 Croats. In the Crisis Staff of the Gornji Vakuf municipality, which was founded by a decision of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf on the 7th of April, 1992, the national composition was as follows: 8 Muslims and 7 Croats. In the Presidency of the municipality, when the Council for National Defence in accordance with the rules of Bosnia and Herzegovina in force at the time came to be called the Presidency of the municipality, there were 11 individuals, 6 of whom were Muslims and 5 of whom were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd then like to ask you a few questions as to issues that came up during the Defence examination of you Monday and Tuesday. Firstly, you said yesterday that you and Mr. Praljak know each other, and I believe you used the words "from that time." When did you first get to know Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met General Praljak for the first time in Uskoplje in 1993. It was on the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Have you had any contact with Mr. -- or General Praljak after that first meeting in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war I didn't meet him again, but after the war I saw General Praljak on -- on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: To first go back to the August 1993 meeting, what were the circumstances of you meeting him at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in town, in the part of town where the majority of the population was Croatian. It was in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. And the circumstances were such that at the time the HVO forces, who were withdrawing the previous night -- who had been withdrawing the previous night in the face of the Muslim forces attack, they had started returning to certain defence lines in the town and around the town, and they were led by General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of whether General Praljak was in the Gornji Vakuf area during 1992 and the first months of 1993 up until the 1st of August when you met him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So does that mean you're not aware of him being there? You don't know whether he was there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You said you met General Praljak also after that 1st August of 1993 meeting after the war. Was that socialising? Was it coincidence? Would you consider him an acquaintance of yours? Could you be a little bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time after the war, I was elected to the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there were a number of demonstrations or assemblies of ours, and General Praljak would attend them as a guest, and we would see each other on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So these were HDZ gatherings? Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said elective assemblies or meetings, and the members of the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina would meet. Mr. Praljak wouldn't attend them because he wasn't a member of the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correction: The witness did not say "demonstrations" but "meetings."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Did you meet with General Praljak or his counsel prior to testifying in The Hague either when you were here last time at the beginning of October or now?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to coming to The Hague, I did not have any contact with the Defence team representing General Praljak. When I came to The Hague for the first time to testify, I didn't do that for reasons that are familiar to you. I met the assistant of Mr. Praljak's lead attorney, and she is present here in the -- in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that was -- that was the first time you came to The Hague, so in October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. And now this weekend before coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. A different question that was also an issue that was touched upon yesterday as well. You were asked about international presence in Gornji Vakuf, about UNPROFOR presence in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, and as far as I recall, you couldn't confirm that there was UNPROFOR presence in town at that time. An officer of UNPROFOR with BritBat, which was the force that was in Gornji Vakuf at the time, he testified here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And the transcript reference for counsel is page 8427, and that should be from line 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And, Witness, he was asked whether it was correct that he served as an intelligence officer for the Cheshire Regiment from early November 1992 to early May 1993 at Gornji Vakuf, and his answer was: "Yes, that is correct." Does that jog your memory? Does it comply with your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. At that time, towards the end of 1992 up until the 11th of January, 1993, I did not meet such representatives, and I didn't talk to such representatives. So this is not something that I could confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So you're saying that you can -- you can neither confirm nor deny; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Confirm or deny what? He hasn't met anybody up until January 11th, 1993, so what can he confirm or deny? He just indicated that he hasn't met anyone. The question is unclear. I don't know what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My point is, Witness, this Williams who was an officer with the Cheshire Regiment, he says that he was in Gornji Vakuf from November 1992 until May 1993. And if I understand you correctly, you didn't meet him or any other representatives of the UNPROFOR force in 1992 up until January 1993, and that means you can neither confirm nor deny what Mr. Williams said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, this is how I would answer the question. I said this, and I'll repeat it: In the autumn of 1992, right up until the 11th of January, 1993, while I was working as the president of the executive committee of the Assembly of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf and while performing my duties as a member of the Presidency in Gornji Vakuf, I didn't meet such people. I didn't speak to them. From the 11th of January, 1993, onwards, I no longer had such a role that would allow me to meet such people, so during that period of time I didn't see any such people, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Do you know whether UNPROFOR representatives were there in Gornji Vakuf prior to January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday I put a question to you because I was surprised that you hadn't seen them, because we know through the testimony of this officer that he was involved in intelligence, and when you're involved in intelligence you should at least go and meet the political officials or administrative officials of the place where one works, unless one is a secret agent such as James Bond, but that wasn't the case because he was in uniform. So that's what is a little surprising, that you didn't see him, and he told us, "I was involved in intelligence." So we have a mystery there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 11th of January, 1993, I was at a meeting with representatives of the European Community. These were people in white, dressed in white. I am the president of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. Mr. Abdulah Garaca attended the meeting. There were similar meetings that were held earlier on with representatives of the European Union or, rather, with monitors, as we called them. But as for members of the forces that you have asked me about, I had no contact with such individuals, and I cannot confirm that they were there during the period of time that Madam Prosecutor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on. I'd like to go back to a few documents that you looked at with -- during Mr. Karnavas's direct examination yesterday. You should have the binder still with the documents that Mr. Karnavas showed you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at Exhibit number 1D 01696. Can you remember that document from yesterday, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Can you remember having looked at that document with Mr. Karnavas here in court?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So this is a 31st of July, 1992, Gornji Vakuf Executive Committee conclusion, and as was read out by Mr. Karnavas yesterday, I believe, it says in number 1: "The Gornji Vakuf municipal Executive Committee agrees with the installation of the equipment for receiving the HTV signal on the Gornji Vakuf TV repeater provided there is no interference with the TVBH signal." We see your signature, and we see that copies are provided, number 4 there, the SDA, Party of Democratic Action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Then I'd like you to go to Exhibit 1D 01789. That should in the same binder. That's a document going from the president of the Gornji Vakuf SDA to Gornji Vakuf HDZ, and we see up in the right-hand corner that the date is 30 -- excuse me, 23rd of November, 1992. Do you remember that document from the examination by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And it says here from the SDA: "With reference to your request for authorisation to install an HTV, Croatian television, signal receiver ..." And your request, would that be the HDZ request?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The HDZ request is not at all what one has in mind here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But the letter goes to Gornji Vakuf HDZ, doesn't it? And it would then be -- wouldn't it be natural to say your request, that that would be the HDZ request?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that the addressee is the HDZ in Gornji Vakuf. However, Mr. Abdulah Topcic, the then president of the Gornji Vakuf SDA, did not want to communicate or speak with civilian representatives of the HVO, in this case with Mr. Ivan Saric, who sent a request to the Executive Committee of the municipality about the possibility of installing equipment on the TV relay so that one could follow the Croatian television programme in the area. This is why Mr. Topcic changed the -- the name so to put it. He only wanted to speak to representatives of the HDZ, and the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf didn't send him this request, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So you're saying the request came from the HVO, or when getting back to him, he -- Abdulah Topcic addressed the reply to the HDZ. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I should point out that the HVO did not send a request to the SDA but to the Executive Committee of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And we can see down left on this document that the Executive Committee is copied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Continuing from where I was reading from the document, it says: "...we hereby inform you that the party has neither the authority nor the right to authorise this," which I understand is the instalment of an HTV signal receiver, "because the relay is owned by the BH RTV, who should, therefore, be approached in view of the above." When you were asked by Mr. Karnavas about this letter - that would be Mr. Karnavas on pages 25 to 26 of yesterday's transcript - you said, Mr. Batinic: "This letter by the president of the SDA for Gornji Vakuf municipality does not respect of the conclusion of the Executive Council of the municipality; and at the same time, the armed forces are being asked, probably of the BH army, of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion, to prevent any attempt to mount a signal to receive the Croatian television." However, what I just read out is -- my understanding is that the SDA says one has to contact the BH RTV in this matter because the party has neither the authority nor the right to authorise such instalment. Isn't that correct, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. The RTV of Bosnia-Herzegovina did own the TV relay. However, at the time it was not possible to have contact with those who managed the RTV in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a result, the HVO in Gornji Vakuf contacted the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Gornji Vakuf, and after the conclusion of the Executive Committee of the Gornji Vakuf municipality of the 27th of July, 1992, that was almost four months later, and after the equipment was not installed but everyone insisted on having it installed, after all of this the SDA confirms here that they don't admit the conclusions of the legitimate body of the authorities of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But isn't this the SDA voicing its opinion on the conclusion of the Executive Committee? The SDA was copied in that letter from the Executive Committee as we saw. There's nothing improper in the SDA voicing its opinion, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing improper for the SDA to express its opinion, but what is inappropriate is for this letter to be addressed to the armed forces of, in those days, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereby they are in a sense being assigned the task of preventing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can hear Mr. Scott making comments. Perhaps he could refrain. If he wishes to send notes to his colleague, fine, but there's sort of a running commentary. As the witness is testifying, Mr. Scott is making comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, if I have been too vocal about it, and I will try to lower my voice if that is indeed a problem. I'm sure the witness has not been influenced in the slightest, but nonetheless, I will lower my voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Back to what you last said, Mr. Batinic, this letter, however, from the SDA, it's not addressed to any armed forces, is it? We can see there's a copy to Gornji Vakuf OS and also to the RTV BH, but it is addressed to the Gornji Vakuf HDZ, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, in the title the indication is who the addressee is of this text, that is the HDZ of Gornji Vakuf. It is also addressed to the armed forces, in brackets, the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion, and the formation that had such a name was only a unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And what you're referring to, Mr. Batinic, when you say "addressed to the arm forces," that is the copy to the Gornji Vakuf OS that we see in the left-hand lower corner of the letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to a different document. We're still in the same binder. This is number 1D 01699. This is -- we can see in the right-hand corner, upper corner, it's from 4th of May, 1993. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. The upper corner is a handwritten insertion, and you're quite right. The date is the 29th of April, 1993. It's a conclusion signed by the president of the Presidency, and it says under conclusion: "All Croat officials relieved of their duties in administrative organs hereby lose their status of administrative officials until a final agreement has been reached on the organisation of all organs based on the principle of parity." And copied are Gornji Vakuf HDZ and Gornji Vakuf SDA. Can you remember this document from Mr. Karnavas's examination?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time this document was drafted, I didn't see it; but I did see it later on after this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And can you remember being shown this document by Mr. Karnavas here in court?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So you were asked about this document, and this would be on page 29, Mr. Karnavas, from yesterday, from line 11, and the answer comes a bit further down, and you said -- or you were asked: "Can you explain this conclusion?" And you answered, Mr. Batinic: "Very simple. As two administrations had been set up, which were services for the two peoples, they considered it logical for employees of the joint administration to be fired from the administration that was headed by Mr. Garaca." But, Witness, this is a reference, as far as I can see, to all Croat officials relieved, as in have already been relieved, of their duties in administrative organs. It's not a firing of Croat officials that takes place with this conclusion. Isn't that true from what we're reading?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. If you read this text more closely, you will see that it says they are losing their status of workers in the administration, and a worker in the administration is a person who is an employee of the Municipal Assembly, of any Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I can see that it refers to losing the status of administrative officials, but doesn't it also refer to the Croat officials having been relieved? It says relieved at an earlier stage of their duties.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here who were working until being relieved. Now, when exactly they were relieved, when the decisions to relieve them were passed, I don't know. It is a fact this is the decision of a single ethnic Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to a different document, and this is a document that was brought up by Ms. Alaburic yesterday, and that should be in the binder that you got from Mr. Petkovic's Defence counsel. I think that should be the right one. And I'd ask you to look up number 3D 00511, please. Do you remember that document from Ms. Alaburic's examination yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I know you have the B/C/S version in front of you. There is also an English version where it says that the month that this conclusion was made is illegible, meaning that we can't read the month. Could you please have a look at the B/C/S version, at the date that's in the upper right corner. Is it correct that that appears to refer to 11,7, as in Roman numerals, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what it says here, since there's the number 11, then comma, number 7, and then Roman numeral II, and then dot, and then 92.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yet another document. This is in the binder that you got from Ms. Nozica from Mr. Stojic's Defence yesterday, and that should be the pink one that's to your right. And I'd ask you to look up document -- or Exhibit number P 01102, please. Can you remember this document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you about one specific issue. You see in the first paragraph, and that was also read out to you yesterday, a reference to soldiers from the Ludvig Pavlovic Unit. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: The Ludvig Pavlovic Unit, that wasn't a local Gornji Vakuf unit, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but it did have members from Gornji Vakuf who were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now go into a couple of the incidents in Gornji Vakuf and issues about Gornji Vakuf that you also talked about yesterday, and they would be -- those documents that I'm going to show you would be in Mr. Karnavas's binder. So the big binder from yesterday. But there's a Prosecution binder to the right of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And we should have all the documents that I now will be referring to in that binder so you don't have to change around. And I'll ask you to look at Exhibit number 1D 00208. Actually, there are two -- two binders. So that might be in the second one. It should be in the second one. It's a report from Mr. Ivan Saric, and it says: "...on incidents that took place in the Gornji Vakuf municipality." Can you remember that document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And I'll read out to you, that would be the fourth paragraph, but I think also Mr. Karnavas touched upon yesterday. It starts with: "On the morning of Wednesday, 21st of October, 1992, something really did start to happen. One could feel it the most on the streets of Gornji Vakuf. People moved only in 'their part of town.' Well-armed soldiers of the HVO and the BH army were seen at every corner. The faces of the people were full of fear. Rumours were going around that one or the other had already captured some points in the town, bilateral disarmament had started, and so on. Zdravko Batinic and Fabijan Trbara, members of the Gornji Vakuf HVO, could feel and see all this for themselves since they were in the centre of the town at the time (from 0830 hours to 0900 hours). An explanation for what they found such a surprising turn of events was given to them by the representatives the BH army (Hanefija Prijic aka Paraga and his commander Fahrudin Agic). According to them, the reason for such a situation was the passage of an armed HVO unit through Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Prozor towards Novi Travnik on the night between Tuesday and Wednesday. Since at the time the president of the Gornji Vakuf HVO was not in Gornji Vakuf, Batinic and Trbara, as members of the Gornji Vakuf HVO, took upon themselves the obligation and responsibility to calm the situation down and remove the possibility of a conflict that seemed imminent." And if I understood you correctly yesterday when this report was presented to you, you confirm the events but not the fact that it says here you were a member of the Gornji Vakuf HVO. Is that correctly understood by me?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And we can see that this report from Saric, it goes to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, to the Croatian Defence Council. Why would Mr. Saric, who was the president of the HVO, feel the need to report on these incidents to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the territory of Gornji Vakuf municipality, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Defence Council did not wish any kind of incidents to take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But why would he report to the central authorities? Why would he present you as an HVO member and the HVO members as someone taking charge of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saric was de jure the president of the HVO as the administrative and executive authority for the municipality of Gornji Vakuf appointed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, and it was his task and duty to report to the Presidency of the HZ HB and, therefore, also the HVO about all events of significance in the territory he was in and for which he was appointed. As for his statement that Zdravko Batinic - that is I myself - was a member of the HVO as a civilian administrative and executive authority, that is not true because Zdravko Batinic never de jure or de facto was ever a member of the HVO, of the civilian or administrative authority. Nobody appointed me to that position. I never received any decision to that effect. We did discuss this thing, this possibility, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: When Mr. Saric makes the representation that HVO members are calming down the situation, would that have been an attempt to show to others in the HZ HB hierarchy that Mr. Saric had actually established a civilian authority which was in fact functioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It calls for speculation. How can the gentleman opine on what Mr. Saric had in mind when he did this? He's being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd like a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, Mr. President. This is the quote from the amended 65 ter summary from Mr. Karnavas on behalf of -- or representing Mr. Batinic's testimony, and I tried to ask open questions to start with, but the quote that I just presented is from the amended 65 ter summary. So I might present it in that sense to the witness, then ask him whether that is correct that he said so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may put the question, the more so as this document shows that Mr. Batinic played a certain role at this point in time, and we need to know why he played such a role and what the context was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll first go back to what I was saying to you just before Karnavas took the floor, Mr. Batinic, and this is from the 65 ter summary, which is a summary that we get from the counsel of Mr. Prlic stating what your testimony will be about before you come to court, and what I quoted was from there, and I'm asking you now whether the quote that I will now repeat, whether that is correct, if that was your understanding. "He" - that would be you - "has no idea why Saric is embellishing, but he thinks this may be an attempt to show to others in the HZ HB hierarchy that he had actually established a civilian authority which was, in fact, functioning." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So that would -- I understand you correctly, then, that Mr. Saric reports to his superiors upwards in the HZ HB hierarchy, and it's important for him to show that the civilian local HVO in Gornji Vakuf is functioning?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Saric thought important, but it is a fact that what I said today in the courtroom is true. If I may have a minute to explain what is written here towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. It is not true that Mr. Trbara convened any meeting together with me. On that morning, the atmosphere was reaching boiling point in town, and the text describing it by Mr. Saric in his report regarding incidents between the 19th and the 31st of October, 1992, is correct. However, at the time and on that day in the territory of the municipality, the president of the Presidency of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, Mr. Muhamed Palalic, was not physically present, and for -- due to this, I felt it my responsibility to take some steps to avoid any kind of incident taking place. Through the postman or the courier of the municipality, I sent some 20 invitations for a meeting at the Radusa Hotel, a meeting of the most responsible representatives of the Croatian people, prominent figures in social life, the commander of the armed forces of the HVO, as well as the leading representatives of the Muslim people and the commander of the armed forces of the TO or the BH army, whatever it was at the time. We did have a meeting at the Radusa Hotel. The debate was extremely useful, and at the end it was agreed that through equipment which could be installed at the TV relay, Zdravko Batinic as the president of the executive council of the Municipal Assembly should address the people as well as Dr. Mihad Edzelovic the most influential member of the SDA in those days for Gornji Vakuf, and that is what we did. We made a joint statement for the citizens of Gornji Vakuf on local television, and tensions eased, and on that day nothing happened. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions for this document, but I'll leave it to the Trial Chamber's -- Trial Chamber if they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: A different document, Mr. Batinic, on -- on the same issue. This would be in the first -- the big binder that's to your right. And I'd like you to look up Exhibit P 01184, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could somebody help me, because I don't seem to be able to find my way around these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: The usher will give you a hand.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's so many papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: It's 01184. Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And if you look first at the -- at the last page just to get the date right. That's the second-to-last page of the document. There is written 18th of January, 1993. If you can't find it in your binder, it should be on the screen in front of you. If you see the handwritten passage down to your right.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And if you back to the first page, we see up to the upper-left corner that this is from the office of the president of the Croatian Defence Council, and we see that it goes to the HVO Croatian Defence Council command to Croatian Defence Council of the municipality and to Croatian population of the Gornji Vakuf municipality. And if you look down on that page, you see that it's from Dr. Jadranko Prlic, president of the HVO of the HZ HB. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: It's addressed to the Croatian population of the Gornji Vakuf municipality, so I'll read out a part of it, so I'm asking you to pay attention. It says: "Gornji Vakuf. "At its today's special session, the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna discussed political and security conditions in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and especially in the area of your municipality. "From the reports of the Defence Section of the HVO of the HZ Herceg-Bosna, then from the contacts with your officials and officers, as well as on the basis of reports of objective media, it is obvious that the Muslim forces are intending to take over the rule to enable HVO defensive activities and then, by applying terror, to cause an exodus of the Croatian people from that area. "Giving full support to resisting such intentions, the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is determined to provide you with any form of help, including the force and combat readiness of the armed forces of the HVO. You are not alone, and you will not be left at the mercy of the Muslim extremists who seem to have armed themselves for settling accounts with the Croatian people instead of joining in the common struggle against the Serbian-Chetnik aggressor. "The Croatian Defence Council and the entire Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are with you." When Prlic says in this letter that the HVO of the HZ HB gives full support to you in Gornji Vakuf and will provide you with any form of help, including the force and combat readiness of the armed forces of the HVO, did you have this -- or did you know about this at the time? Was that your view, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was behind you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were firmly convinced that we wouldn't be alone in that difficult armed conflict in the month of January 1993. We expected the assistance of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, all forms of assistance. At the time, what we most needed was military assistance. Forces in the HVO were attacked by several thousand members of the ABiH from a number of directions, in the town from the direction of Bugojno, and so on and so forth. And without forces assisting, Herceg-Bosna -- Herceg-Bosna couldn't have defended itself, and I believe that this is why Mr. Prlic sent this letter of support to the Croatian people in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Can you remember having had referred to you the particular -- this particular letter, or is this a view, an opinion you had based on other sources?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this letter before, but I don't know which sources you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You said that you were firmly convinced that you wouldn't be left alone and that you would have the support of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do I understand you correctly that that was the view you had based on -- well, on different -- on different sources, on different documents or discussions that you'd -- you'd had with other people?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I based this opinion above all on the fact that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had been founded to protect the Croatian people in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whenever the Croatian population, any part of it, was threatened or attacked, the HZ HB was prepared to assist those people, wherever they were, if this was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more document on the October events, October 1992 events, that I would like to show to you, and that should be in the same binder that you have. It's P 00712. If you look at the first page, you can see that it is a letter or a report to the military police administration in Mostar, Mr. Valentin Coric: "Subject: Report on events in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf municipalities," and it's from the commander of the 2nd military police battalion, Zdenko Andabak. And if you look up to the right-hand corner, the date is the 6th of November. You've talked about the October events in Gornji Vakuf. There were some incidents in Prozor in October 1992, as well, weren't there? On the 23rd of October, there was fighting in Prozor. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And the HVO took over Prozor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that that's correct. After the fighting in the town of Prozor, the HVO had in a certain sense taken control of the town of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then you're referring to the October fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date do you have in mind when you say October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: 23rd of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, 1992, as far as I know the initial clash had only just started, the clash that involved the neighbouring municipality, a clash between TO and HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But can we agree that - and I'm using your words - after the fighting in the town of Prozor in October 1992, the HVO had in a certain sense taken control of the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, the clashes began in the area of the Prozor municipality; but it was on the 24th of October, 1992, that the HVO took control of the area of Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you for that specification, Mr. Batinic. This fighting in Prozor, did that increase tensions in Gornji Vakuf, as well, being a neighbouring municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. With your leave, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions first to this document.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But start with that, and we'll see how we go. I read out what this report is about. I assume you don't know that report. You don't recognise the document itself, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I would, however, like to read out a few portions from this report and to ask you whether that complies with your knowledge and with what you saw on the ground at this time in October 1992, and I'd like you to go to page 5 in the B/C/S version. That should also be page 5 in the English version. That's the page that starts dealing with Gornji Vakuf municipality. Have you found that, Mr. Batinic? It starts with a section on Prozor, this report, and then goes on to deal with Gornji Vakuf on page 5 of the version you have. It should be on the screen in front of you also. Are you able to find it? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Sorry, it should be page 4 of the B/C/S version. But you see it, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: This is a report, a continuation on the report on Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, and there's first a reference to the 19th of October, 1992. It says: "The command of the Gornji Vakuf Main Staff issued a decision on placing members of the military police at full combat readiness." Were you aware of that decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I didn't think he understood that that was a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll repeat it, Mr. Batinic. You see there's first a reference to the 19th of October, 1992, and it says, at the time, there was a decision on placing members of the military police at full combat readiness, and I was asking you, at the time, were you aware of that decision?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Then it goes on to the 23rd of October: "Full combat readiness was also ordered for all Gornji Vakuf HVO units." Were you aware of that decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this decision of the 23rd of October, 1992 -- of the 29th of October, but I myself realised that tension had increased to such an extent that both sides in Gornji Vakuf and around Gornji Vakuf were at full combat readiness when it came to their armed forces. That concerned the Territorial Defence and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And this realisation of yours, would that be something you had by the 23rd of October? Am I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 23rd of October, 1992. You understood me correctly. On that same day, we had two meetings in order to prevent an armed conflict of any kind from breaking out in the area of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I could ask you to go back to the document. The next entry is the 24th of October, but I'm moving on, and if you see the next entry after that, it's the 25th of October. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And right above 25th of October, there's the sentence that says the following: "Following the street fighting, HVO members captured all the factories and took control of them." And this should then be the 24th of October. Were you aware of the HVO members having captured all the factories in Gornji Vakuf and taking control of them on the 24th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll partially answer your question by saying yes -- or, rather, no, but I don't have to explain that [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to ask you to be a bit more specific if you can. What's the yes part, and what is the no part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman indicated he did want to explain, not that he did not want to explain. In the record it shows that he did not want to explain. Yes -- partially yes, no, and then it looks like it says that he doesn't want to explain. He does want to explain. That's why the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I heard you saying that you didn't want to explain, and I would like you to explain. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say one thing since the witness requested an explanation, that Mr. Karnavas got up before me with his objection, but I think it will be fair to the witness and to everyone else in the courtroom not to read out only parts of this report, because my colleague skips one sentence and reads out the following one, but the events in the report are linked. If the witness was given the opportunity to read through the entire page, he'd be able to understand all the events. In this way, the events are taken out of context, and this confuses the witness because we have events for one day. We have full combat readiness mentioned in this document with regard to both military forces. We see that something was taken over, that there was an armed conflict. This conflict was started, according to this document, by the TO or the BH army, and then the response was to see certain features. This all makes sense, and as a result I don't think it's a good idea to selectively read through the document because we have a chronological description of the events and of the acts of both sides, and it's also linked to other events in other municipalities, for example, in the municipality of Travnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see how what I'm doing now is different from what is the usual practice in this case, and if Mr. Karnavas who brought in the witness wants to go back to any parts of this report, he can certainly do so on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there is something called the rule of completeness. You can't take something out of context, and I would suggest giving the gentleman an opportunity to at least look at the entire text in context. He can look at it himself, and then he can answer the question, but, you know, there is such a thing as the rule of completeness, and I'm sure that my colleague Mr. Scott would agree with me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, the document is not one the witness knows, but perhaps he is familiar with the context. So to avoid this entire debate, one should have asked him, first of all, whether he knew how these events took place, if he had perfect knowledge or partial knowledge of these events, and then you could have continued by referring to certain particular issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll take that on board, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If we go back to where we were, Mr. Batinic, it was the 24th of October, as I referred to before quoting from the report, and we have heard you testify about how you were in Gornji Vakuf at the time in October and how you were involved in some of the incidents there. So I'll ask you again. I know you don't have knowledge about this report in particular, because that's what I asked you initially, but do you have any knowledge -- or did you have any knowledge at the time of the HVO members capturing all the factories in Gornji Vakuf and taking control of them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had to explain this, but first of all I want to deny what you have just said. I didn't participate in any incidents at the time in Gornji Vakuf -- or, rather, not during the period -- or not on the 24th of October, 1992. I was one of those who tried to prevent incidents at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I may just on that. There might have been a translation issue here because what I was referring to was actually your involvement in what you said, what you talked about, calming down the tension. So that was my -- that was my intention, to refer to that. So if you could please go on and explain your answer to my question regarding the factories.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the entrance to Gornji Vakuf when coming from the direction of Bugojno in 1992, there were four companies to the right of the main road and at the entrance to Gornji Vakuf. There was a construction company called Kozara. There was a factory for processing metal called Tom. There was the Unis factory and the Borac factory. These settlements are linked to part town inhabited by Croats who were in the majority there. In the factories and behind the factories at that time, between the 24th and 25th of October, 1992, there was no fighting, nor was it necessary for the HVO to fight for the factories; but as a preventive measure, they deployed a minor number of men so that TO forces would not enter the factories through Vrbas. There was no fighting and no seizing of the factories by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So am I understanding correctly, then, that -- and I know you haven't seen the document before, but you -- your knowledge at the time related to this report or in -- as regards the issues of this report on the factories, you believe Mr. Andabak was referring to the factories you testified about just now?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area we have some other factories, but none of them were in the area of conflict in relation to Mr. Andabak's mission, apart from the ones I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If we go on to the 25th of October -- can you see there's a reference to the 25th of October right below what I read out now?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Then there's a reference to the 26th of October. At the time, you were still in Gornji Vakuf, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 20th of June, 1992, I was in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: What I was referring to was the 26th of October, 1992, which is the date in the report. On the 26th of October, 1992, were you then in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to read out what it says in the report here about 26th of October and ask you whether that complies with your knowledge, being present in Gornji Vakuf at the time. "HVO units took the Gornji Vakuf MUP, Ministry of the Interior, building and post, which they still have under their control." Does that comply with your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but I should point out from the building of the MUP and the post office in the part of town -- well, it was in the part of town where the Croats were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And the MUP building or the M-U-P building, is that the same as the police station, the same building?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We called it the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Were these buildings under the control of the ABiH prior to the 26th of October? In other words, did the HVO, on the 26th of October, take over control of the MUP building and the post office?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The TO forces weren't in the MUP building. They weren't in the post office, either. When it says they took -- or perhaps this hasn't been phrased correctly. One should have said they were in the MUP building and the post office, but they were on the margins of that part of town where Croats are the majority. So it was logical for HVO forces to deploy these margins of inhabited places, to protect the Croatian people in those places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a question here. How would -- how do you explain the fact that Mr. Andabak finds it important enough to say in this report the HVO took over the MUP, et cetera, when you say that they were there anyway? From whom did they take it over, from whom? Was -- was there no act that could be described at all as a taking-over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I knew, Your Honour, there was no fighting to take control of the public security station and the post office. At that time, it was somehow logical for each side to remain in their part of the town, in part of town where the Croats were in the majority. That's where the HVO would remain; and in the part of town where the Muslims were in the majority, members of the TO, well, remained in that part of town. It was important for a sort of imaginary line not to be crossed by either of the sides, an imaginary demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hear this, but it does not quite answer the question. "Taking over" means that you gain possession in a large sense of something of which before you did not have possession. So after the 26th -- as of the 26th, we must conclude from this passage, assuming that it is a true report, that the HVO had "possession" of MUP. Who was in possession before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the public security station, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And would they be mixed? Would there also be some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The public security station was mixed in ethic terms. So there were Muslim policemen who worked there, too, naturally. But if I may, just one sentence. As soon as the tension in the town was felt, everyone took shelter in "their own part of town." So the HVO forces or colleagues, policemen who were Croats, didn't have to forcibly expel Muslim colleagues from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that has clarified the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our break now, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and everyone in the courtroom, counsel. Your Honour, I regret needing to interrupt at the moment the cross-examination of my colleague, Ms. Moe, and I apologise to her as well as everyone else for that. However, there's something I do need to raise this week, and I put it off -- I intentionally put it off not to take the time during the Defence questioning, but I feel that I cannot -- I feel that I cannot put it until later this week given -- depending what the schedule might be and what the Chamber's ruling might be, so I ask the Court's indulgence for a few moments to address an issue relating to next week's witness, Mr. Tomic, who you know is returning. Your Honour, my concern in part, and I say in part, arises out of what I've heard, and I'm not being critical in any way, and I hope Mr. Karnavas will not take this to mean more than what I intend it to mean. I've heard Mr. Karnavas to say on several occasions that he would like two hours for direct -- for redirect examination. Now, ultimately, of course, of course, that is in the Trial Chamber's hands, and the Trial Chamber can choose to give Mr. Karnavas two hours or three hours or four hours. But the concern the Prosecution has, Your Honour, is that there needs to be some proportionality and some parity, some fairness here with the amount of time provided for Defence questioning and the time provided to the Prosecution for its questioning. And again, I raise this today because with the greatest respect to the Chamber, I would appreciate a ruling as soon as possible on my request to the Chamber, because it will affect, it will directly effect our continuing preparations for next week's witness, and it's not something that can be simply resolve at 2.15 next Monday. After -- we will have no opportunity at that point to respond or to -- to adjust our preparations accordingly concerning a witness that everyone in the courtroom recognises is an important witness. I think Mr. Karnavas himself has indicated this is one of the most important witnesses. So if that's the case, Your Honour, ever -- evermore reason why the Prosecution should have a fair opportunity to question the witness as well. I hope that I -- I'll ask -- I think it's very important, Your Honour, and it will take more than one minute because I do have some information that I do want to put before the Chamber, and I have a short handout to be provided to the Judges and, of course, to the Defence counsel. If the usher can assist us, please. I'll give everybody just a couple of seconds to orient yourself to the document. Your Honour, the top of the page, this is a summary of the Tomic situation to date, if you will. To date, the direct examination and the co-accused examination has taken a total of 11 hours and 17 minutes, and these -- all these times, I should say, just so everyone's clear, all these times come directly from the registry. They're not -- they're not the Prosecution's invention. This all comes from the time records kept by the registry. The total time with Mr. Tomic by the Defence to date is 11 hours, 7 minutes. The Chamber had indicated that the Prosecution cross could be eight hours. Mr. Karnavas has requested two hours of direct -- of redirect. Now, if that -- if that were to play out, if that were to become the situation, I would note, Your Honours, that that would mean that with this witness the Defence will have been given a total of 13 hours and 7 minutes, and the Prosecution only 8 hours. Now, keep that in mind for a moment. Now, we went back and looked at some of the other redirects in this case, and to be fair, we looked at the longest redirect in the Prosecution case and the longest redirect in the Defence cases to date. In the Prosecution case, the longest witness was Witness EA, the longest redirect. The direct of that witness took 6 hours, 46 minutes. The total Defence time, note, Your Honours, the total Defence time was 10 hours. Redirect was 56 minutes. So on a total -- in response to a total Defence questioning of 10 hours - 10 hours, not 8 hours, 10 hours - the Prosecution had 56 minutes for redirect. At the end of the day, again, you'll see that in that particular instance, total, the Defence had 10 hours; the Prosecution had 7 hours and 42 minutes. Now, in terms of the longest redirect in the Defence case to date, Mr. Perkovic, the direct and co-accused took 7 hours. The Prosecution cross-examination was 4 hours, 50 minutes, once again, substantially less than the Defence time. Redirect was 40 minutes. So after 7 hours of Defence questioning, an additional 40 minutes of redirect in that particular case. And again, you'll see the total time, the total defence time, 7 hours and 40 minutes; total Prosecution time, 4 hours and 50 minutes, almost 3 hours, almost 3 hours less than the time given to the Defence. Now, Your Honour, these situations unfortunately do not take place in a vacuum; and as Mr. Karnavas always likes to say, if we put these matters in context, Prosecution has also from the time records kept by the registry looked at some more general time periods. In the Prosecution case, in the Prosecution case, the Prosecution had 30 per cent of court time; Defence had 37 per cent of court time. Substantially more. In the Prosecution's case - I emphasise - in the Prosecution's case, the Defence got more time in the Prosecution case than the Prosecution got. Substantially more. And in the Defence cases to date, the Defence has used 37 per cent of the total court time, and the Prosecution has received 27 per cent. Substantially, very substantially, less. With great respect to the Chamber, the practices of the Chamber and the times being allowed under all these various practices and rules is systematically - and I underline the word "systematically" - working at the disadvantage, the substantial disadvantage of the Prosecution. We are given with every witness, with virtually every witness, every aspect of the case, substantially less time than the Defence is getting. Systematically, consistently. Now, Your Honour, we think that's fundamentally unfair for a number of reasons. I won't go into all of them. Some of the discussions, we've had before. Prosecution in this case, in the Prlic trial, is being repeatedly, systematically and substantially given less time than the Defence. Now, if we're being asked to -- to cut our times repeatedly, I don't think that's fair, Your Honour. Now, let me -- let me put this in context again. My issue is less to do with the amount of time given to Mr. Karnavas. If the Chamber wants to give Mr. Karnavas five hours of redirect, that's within the Trial Chamber's discretion. Give him five hours, but there has to be some proportionality, Your Honour, some fairness with the amount of time given to the Prosecution to examine the same witness. Now, just to make this a little bit more topical, something that was raised earlier this week in response to, I think, some questions put by Judge -- comments made by Judge Trechsel. The issue of confederation, of a possible confederation with Croatia came up, and it sounded -- what the response -- what I took from the Chamber's reaction is, this is something the Chamber has not -- or at least some of the Chamber has not heard a lot about or has been presented. That is an issue, that is an issue that is in my outline to go into with the witness Tomic. It's there. It's been there. I will not get to it. I will not be able to cover that topic on the time that's presently allowed. So, Your Honour, there has to be some fairness here. We are consistently being given less time. Look -- and also, I gave you the comparisons of the redirects concerning other cases. Nothing has been granted approaching two hours, nothing. It's never -- redirect has never exceeded an hour, has never, ever exceeded an hour. Now, again, though, give Mr. Karnavas however time -- much time you want, but give the Prosecution a fair amount of time as well. What we specifically seek, Your Honours, is to have at least, to have at least one-half of the time taken by the other accused, which would -- Tomic was 3 hours and 10 minutes. Half of that, half of that - which leaves the Prosecution still at a significant disadvantage; we will still have had substantially less time with this witness than the Defence - would be half of the additional co-accused questioning, half of that time would be an hour and 35 minutes. That is half the time that they took. Your Honour, in terms of completing the cross-examination of Mr. Tomic and so that we can prepare for next week, the Prosecution asks the Chamber to grant it an additional one hour and 35 minutes to examine this witness for all the reasons stated. I would be greatly -- I would greatly appreciate, Your Honour; with the greatest respect to all of you -- all of the Judges, I would greatly respect -- appreciate, excuse me, a ruling so that -- before next week so that we can prepare accordingly. And again, as I see Mr. Karnavas get to his feet, my concern is less with the time -- give Mr. Karnavas as much time as you want. Give him as much time as you want, but give the Prosecution a fair amount of time as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for the generosity that Mr. Scott is expressing. Two points or maybe three or maybe more. First, essentially, 80 per cent of the -- the submission today had nothing to do with redirect but, rather, had to do with the request for additional time for cross-examination; and I think in that instance the Prosecution should, as we have done in the past, pitch his case, make his position known why they need the additional time in this instance, and give us some concrete basis upon which we can either take a position and, more importantly, the Trial Chamber can also make a decision. So essentially, let's -- let's get down to brass tacks, as they say. This is really a request for additional time. As far as redirect examination, I think Mr. Scott may be wrong. I believe Zoran Buntic was a little bit longer than 40 minutes. That was my recollection. So my longest redirect probably was more than 40. I say that because I make no apologies for a redirect that may take more than 40 or 50 minutes or an hour. Redirect has a specific purpose. Obviously, I cannot go outside the scope of the direct examination. I think if the Trial Chamber looks over all of the witnesses that I've put forward thus far, I've been -- I've used redirect sparingly, and when I do it's rather targeted. Some Judges may disagree. Of course, my redirect is based on 25 years of experience in the courtroom. So it's based on that. So -- and in the event in any of my redirect it is irrelevant, it is up for the Prosecution to object and, of course, for the Judges to jump in as they normally do to ask questions, why is this relevant, or this is going beyond the cope of the cross-examination. That has not happened. Therefore, I see no problem with that. My biggest concern with -- with the submissions made by Mr. Scott is that he somehow seems to think that we are all holding hands here singing "Kumbaya" on this side, this aisle, this side of the courtroom; and I can assure you we have six different defences. Now, in part, one of the reasons I need additional time is because of certain matters that were brought up by other Defence teams. Now, I can either not address it, or I can address it. Now, it's my duty to my client to address it. And I notice, Judge Trechsel that you're shaking your head a little bit, and I get the feeling that you must think that we are in some kind of a joint enterprise here against the Prosecution. And I can assure you, that is not the case. My enterprise is with my client. To the extent that it might -- I might share some issues with one of the other teams, that's fine; but we don't get together. We don't strategize. We don't plan out my direct examination and say, I won't cover this, you cover that. Anybody that wants to meet a witness, they're free to do so, and that goes with experts as well. We -- in fact, we don't even prevent the Prosecution. If they wanted to meet with any of our witnesses, they're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In fairness, Mr. Karnavas, shouldn't you also remark when I nod? Because you always make a comment when I shake my head, which I have many reasons, not necessarily those which you imagine. But I also often nod my head, and you never remark on that, which is not equitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's true. That's true. If you could nod in favour, is what I'm saying right now, I would most definitely go on record. But in any event, I think the numbers themselves really do not -- cannot assist us that much. I think the Prosecution should simply, you know, make their case that they need additional time for the variety of reasons. The Trial Chamber can do so. I said two hours because that's what I'm thinking at this time based on what I heard and what I'm expecting from the Prosecution. It may take an hour and a half. I do have -- because I have some luxury, in a sense, of more time to prepare my redirect, I will try to be as streamlined as possible; and I can assure you what I will be doing is going from the transcript saying page this, this was mentioned, and if the Trial Chamber wishes in advance for me to present some kind of a -- topics, list of topics of which I'm going to go into redirect with this particular witness because he's been such a long witness, I'm prepared to do that. Not now, because I'm not ready, but I could do that. But I don't -- I frankly think that the Prosecution is -- is using these statistics to somehow show that they're not getting their fair share of the pie, and I don't think that's correct. And when you look at these numbers, and it says 30 per cent Prosecution, 37 Defence. Well, again, there's six different Defences over here, so obviously there's going to be a little extra time. But I don't think that you should look at the numbers. And I might add, there were many witnesses that the Prosecution brought that I never cross-examined, not even a single question. I thanked them for coming here, giving their evidence. So I don't think that we should just go by the numbers. I think the Prosecution should probably give some greater detail, maybe in writing, as to why they need the additional time. The Defence can then make appropriate responses, and then, of course, the Trial Chamber will be in a much better position to assess whether in fact they need additional time. That's all I need to say, and I hope that I wasn't in any way suggesting that the Prosecution should not get additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate. The Chamber is fully au courant. The Prosecution wants an hour and 35 minutes' additional time. Mr. Karnavas has told us that he would need two hours, but I think that is the maximum possible. So for the moment, the other Defences are not involved. Yes, Mr. Stewart or Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please go first, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's quite correct that this principally involves a Prlic witness. However, the submission put forward by my learned friend Mr. Scott is of -- perhaps of wider implication because it deals with the issue of time. Now, it is patently obvious to everybody in this courtroom that neither the Prosecution nor the Defence are completely satisfied with how time has been apportioned in this case. I make no comment on that. Opportunities were there to appeal that, and decisions have been rendered. And without taking a position, of course, it may be a sign of an independent and impartial Chamber that on such a fundamental issue both sides are equally unhappy. But I do take issue with the greatest of respect for the actual basis of my learned friend's application. The time detailed on the sheet handed over is contorted in reality because the time is very much a function of the Prosecution's decision to have a joint trial with six individuals. And when one is looking simply at Tomic, the Prosecution have been given eight hours to cross-examine, whereas all the Defence, Mr. Prlic's counsel and all the accused, have been given 11 hours, so it's more than half. But it's fundamentally in error to start raising -- to start saying that the Chamber is cutting, is cutting the time of the Prosecution, because I don't see what cut has been made by Your Honours to the time given to the Prosecution in relation to this witness or any witnesses, because the time, of course, in re-examination is -- the time has already been allocated to a party. Similarly, when one looks at Witness EA, which my learned friend prays in aid, it's of hardly any utility because every counsel has different approaches to cross-examination and re-examination. The fact that the Prosecution has chosen, has chosen, to spend 56 minutes in re-examination or redirect, to use the American expression as detailed on the sheet, could be -- could have been for a whole variety of reasons, but it's a decision of the Prosecution. If they wanted to spend more time on re-examination out of their time that they were allotted in their case in chief, well, that would have been a reasonable option. Again, re-examination is not at large. Re-examination is always curtailed by the grounds of relevance, and it has to be focused on matters that have arisen in cross-examination. So, Your Honours, I don't see, to be quite candid, any prejudice to the Prosecution on the grounds that they have detailed either that time has been cut by the Trial Chamber that was granted to the Prosecution or that re-examination is conducted for 30 minutes, 40 minutes, or even 2 hours. It has to be relevant, and it has to be within the confines of matters that are raised in cross-examination. On numerous occasions, the Prosecution have said quite correctly very often when interjections have been made by the Defence, this is inappropriate, whatever the arguments of the principle of completeness. The Prosecution say, well, my learned friend can raise this in re-examination. Well, it can't be -- my learned friends can't have it both ways; and in my submission, it would have been perhaps more appropriate, it's a matter for the Prosecution, to simply focus on if they want more time, cogent and compelling arguments can be put forward. Those arguments, in my respectful submission, have not been presented in this present application by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say that I don't really understand why we are running around in a circle. What I am concerned about is that the Chamber made a very specific decision about the time allotted to the Defence about the way in which the time would be calculated for cross-examination; and within the framework of that decision, it was stated that the time given to the Defence for redirect would be detracted from their time, and Mr. Karnavas was told that you can use as much time as you like for the redirect, but later on you will have less time for the direct examination of another witness if you use your time in that way. According to the calculation of time that we are given by the registrar, I see that Mr. Karnavas has still plenty of time that has been allotted to him for his defence. I don't really see what the problem is. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence also specifies what the direct examination is about, what the redirect is about. It has to be within the scope of the cross-examination. So I don't understand what we're discussing. We're spending a lot of time discussing something that has already been decided. I think everything is quite clear, and there is no problems there. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will end with Mr. Stewart now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would just like to -- to stress once again that -- that these are six separate Defences, and the Prosecution presentation of their submission here, again, oversimplifies the matter. It's not just that there's the Prosecution and then there's in this instance Mr. Karnavas's client, because we have our cross-examination, as well, and it isn't just a continuation of direct examination.
