It is -- in almost every instance, it is a cross-examination from our different standpoint because we are a different Defence, so that the re-examination - this applies to Mr. Karnavas at the moment because he's calling witnesses, but it will apply to us when we call our witnesses - our re-examination has to deal with the cross-examination by the Prosecution of our witness and also by cross-examinations by it could be up to five. It's not usually the whole five, but it could be any number of the other Defences. The last point I wish to make is this, that the submission that -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please close your remarks as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is my last point, Your Honour, simply to say that except as a guideline, we do question whether any sort of time limit other than as a guideline is really appropriate for a re-examination, because as Mr. Khan has already commented, it is far simpler for the Trial Chamber to ensure in case of re-examination that it is properly linked, properly arises out of cross-examination. It's a far simpler exercise provided the matters are relevant, provided they do properly arise out of cross-examination by any of the other defendants or the Prosecution. Your Honour should, with respect, not cut off re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the fact that the Prosecution's proposal regards all six Defence counsels, I think we need to express an opinion. First of all, I fully agree with what my colleagues have said in the interests of saving time, but I wish to add just one additional point. From this summary table on the sheet distributed to us by the Prosecution, and the table relates to the total amount of time spent in the Prosecution case, and it is thereby implied that even in the Prosecution case the Defence had more time than the Prosecution. In the opinion of the Prosecution, this is an indication of unfairness towards him. I would just like to say the following: The first point is what my colleagues have already stressed. We don't have one accused here but six accused. Theoretically, we should have had six times more time than him. But as you have said on several occasions, that is not possible, so we -- each of us had a sixth of the total time. A second point, the Prosecution, as you remember well, called more witnesses under 92 ter and expert witnesses, and as a rule on those occasions the Defence was given additional time. The value expressed in time of the written statement was used to estimate roughly how much time the witness would have needed had he spoken viva voce; and in my opinion, this, I think, would explain the 7 per cent that we had extra, plus when we expressly required additional time, but for this we provided arguments, and when those arguments were worthwhile, we were granted that additional time by the Chamber. Now, if the Prosecutor simply wishes additional time to cross-examine the mentioned witness, let him provide the arguments. But to go back again, as my learned friend has mentioned, for us to go round in a circle and to go back to certain fundamental premises of these proceedings is absolutely inappropriate. You have already ruled, and such an approach is a kind of lack of respect for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to be brief, but here, again, is an example. I'm not -- I'm not being critical of the time taken by the Defence in saying this at all. I'm not being critical. I'm just saying, this is a perfect example of -- in this set of submissions, Defence has taken substantially more time to present their issue than the Prosecution has. Your Honour, the proper situation with -- the proper characterisation of the situation here is -- is that, indeed, there is a specific particular issue, the examination of Mr. Tomic, which, indeed, takes place in a -- as part of a larger issue. Excuse me. I don't -- I heard some comments from -- there's a problem or ... Your Honour, again, these are not the Prosecution's numbers. You know, the Defence -- the Defence may not like what the numbers show. There may be various explanations for some of them, but these are the registry's numbers, and they show what they show, and it is the Prosecution case, with the greatest respect to the Chamber, that the Chamber's practices consistently and systematically provide the Prosecution with substantially less time. Now, I'm sorry if that offends either the Chamber or anyone else in the courtroom, but that's what the numbers consistently show. Now, as to -- as to the examinations and -- and the co-accused -- among the co-accused and the person conducting -- the party conducting direct, I won't belabour it, Your Honour. I know the Chamber's heard me say this a number of times. In my view to date, since the Defence cases started in May, in my view there has been virtually or very -- well, virtually none or extremely little of anything that I would consider to be cross-examination or examination adverse -- of an adverse witness or adverse testimony of a witness. They -- Defence counsel may not meet and plan out their six or however many examinations are conducted; but, Your Honour, they have all been essentially -- these have all been treated essentially as common witnesses. The Prosecution then has to respond to the co-accused questioning. We can't simply let that go unaddressed. Ms. Alaburic gets up and raises issues not raised by Mr. Karnavas or expands on them substantially. Ms. Nozica gets up. Mr. Praljak gets up. The Prosecution can't simply have no time to respond to those issues, and we do have to allocate our time. Now, the Defence says, well, there are six of us. Well, we have to divide our time among the six, as well, however many issues that are raised. As termed -- in terms of the length of time of redirect taken for Witness EA, something was said by one of the Defence submissions that, well, the Prosecution should have been given or should have had as much time as reasonable. I think the record will show, Your Honour, that since that was the longest redirect the Prosecution had ever conducted in its own case, I think the record will show that we had to push and pretty much beg to get that much time. It wasn't that we just had an abundance of time to burn. It was a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to stop now. We have understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me finish my comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Conclude rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. I just want to make an important point back -- both in response to something said this morning and something said earlier this week. Mr. Karnavas reminded us earlier this week that the Prosecution has the burden of proof, which is absolutely true, and the Prosecution has never said to the contrary. But I again observe to the Chamber that the party who has the burden of proof in the case, the party who has to prove its case, unlike the Defence, is, again, being given less time than the Defence. We have the burden of proof, and we're being given less time to prove, to meet the burden that we have. Now, in terms of the 1 hour and 35 minutes, Your Honours, we think that that's probably not even enough, but it will certainly be better than what we have now. There's the issue of confederation. There's the other issues of Mr. Prlic's involvement in running the government. There's a number of issues that we would like to address that given the time that allows we will not be able to address in that amount of time, and I can only represent -- as Mr. Karnavas says, I've also been doing this for 30 years -- going on almost 30 years. I have a pretty good instinct as to what time allows, and I can only represent in the greatest good faith to the Chamber that there's no way that I can adequately cover these additional topics in the remaining time. I thank the Court for its consideration. Again, I'm sorry to have taken the time this morning, but I think the record will show the Prosecution's always been reluctant to take any time more than absolutely necessary, and this -- and our view was necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will render a decision. Let's have the witness in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Batinic, you may sit down. The Chamber apologises for having made you wait, but we had to deal with questions raised by the Prosecution and the Defence, and as a result you have been brought back into the courtroom about half an hour later than scheduled. Madam Prosecutor, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like, Mr. Batinic, to go back to another issue that you talked about yesterday - or was it Monday - and that refers to -- I think maybe both days. That refers to the hanging of Croat flags in December or January, December 1992, January 1993. And if I understand you correctly, what you said was that the Croats of Gornji Vakuf raised some flags for the celebration of Christmas and New Year's and that some Muslims took down these flags. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats in Gornji Vakuf put up their national symbols just before Christmas on the 25th of December, 1992. Those symbols are the symbols of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, this irritated some Muslims who took these symbols down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I take what you say on board, but I'd also like to ask you whether there was a particular incident on the 4th of January, 1993 - that was a Monday - involving the raising of a flag by Croats on that particular day in the town of Gornji Vakuf. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I would like to hear from you which Croatian flag you have in mind, the Croatian flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the flag of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll go to a document that I can show you because I wasn't there at the time, so I'll show you an exhibit that refers to this, and I'll ask you to go to the binder that you have in front you to P 01068. That's one of the exhibits in the binder. Do you have the B/C/S version of P 01068 in front of you? This is --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an exhibit that has already been dealt with here in court. It's an information report from the BritBat contingent that I've referred to earlier that was stationed in Gornji Vakuf, and it's from the 6th of January, 1993, and you can see that the headline is "Gornji Vakuf" on the first page there. And just to make that clear, I assume that you can't -- you don't recognise, you don't know this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll read out part of it, and I'll ask you to -- to tell me whether that replies with what your knowledge at the time, and I do recognise that the English copy is quite bad, but I know that this is an exhibit that has been dealt with previously. It's the second paragraph, Mr. Batinic, B/C/S the third paragraph. It starts with: "At approximately 1500 hours on Monday afternoon, the HVO raised a Ustasha flag in the town. The Muslims reacted, and a Bosnian army soldier attempted to remove the flag. An HVO policeman then fired at the Bosnian army soldier in question, resulting in a" -- and I'm having trouble reading that word, but it refers to a "rise in tensions in the town." "A sharp rise in tension in the town." This is a report, as I said, from some internationals that were in Gornji Vakuf at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And for Defence counsel, I know that the date on this was originally the 6th of January, but it was specified to being the 4th of January that it referred to in Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination of Mr. Andrew Williams, so I assume there won't be any dispute on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, what the BritBats here say about the raising of an Ustasha flag in the town of Gornji Vakuf on the 4th of January and the shooting of a Muslim thereafter, did you have any knowledge of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about it at the time, after the 6th of January, 1993, after the Three Kings celebration was over. I knew that one member of the military police fired in the air as a warning or, to be more precise, he wanted to scare a Muslim soldier who was taking down the flag of the Croatian people. As far as the term "Ustasha" is concerned, well, I'd like to clarify something in a few sentences so that everyone can understand this. Unfortunately, at the time there were names used by Muslims for Croats. They would call them Ustashas, and the flag of the Croatian people was treated by some as a Ustasha flag, which is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: A few questions to clarify your answer. Are you aware of a flag being raised on the 4th of January, so being put up on that date, a Croat flag?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian flags of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were put up before the 25th of December, 1992, and they remained up until the holiday period was over -- or, rather, up until the 6th of January, 1993. And it wasn't just a matter of one flag. Flags were frequently taken down by Muslims. That's what we think. That usually happened at night, and then in the morning a new flag would be put up where there were Croatian flags. But for the 4th of January, I can't say for sure that one or two flags were taken down for sure, but after the Three Kings, on the first working day I found out about this shooting or, rather, this warning that the flags of the Croatian people should not be touched.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My question was, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was listening to you. This matter of flags has been evoked on a number of occasions here, so it's nothing new for the Judges. However, there is something that I have just discovered, and I need an answer from you. You seem to be linking this flag to a religious festival. You say that it was put up before the 25th of December, 1992, so you seem to be linking the raising of this flag to a Catholic event because the Croats put it up. In the previous years, 1980, 1985, 1990, were these flags raised up systematically in Gornji Vakuf before the 25th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, does this mean that the member of the international community who drafted his report perhaps made two mistakes? First of all, he referred to a Ustasha flag. Perhaps he should have obtained information; but secondly, he should have checked with you or with the Catholic body whether this flag had a religious connotation. So now you are telling me that traditionally one would put these flags up; one would raise these flags during this period of time and had religious connotations, not political connotations. Have you understood the question? There must have been an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was not possible because of the Communist authorities to use national symbols for festivals, festivities. It was only after the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 18th of November, 1991, that the newly elected authorities allowed each people to celebrate their religious festivals by displaying their national symbols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I have understood you correctly, in December 1991 this flag had been raised without any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. In 1991 and in 1990, as well, and then naturally in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: To follow up on the President's questions, Mr. Batinic, the flags that you say were raised for Christmas, New Year 1992, were they the flags of the Bosnian -- the flag of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the flags of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So that would be the flag that you were shown yesterday by Mr. Karnavas during his examination, would it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And am I understanding you correctly that you were aware of flags being raised for Christmas and New Year's, but you're not aware of a particular raising of flags on the 4th of January? Is that the correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the 4th of January, 1993, too, but if you were following me, I said that the national symbols of the Croats put up before the religious holiday for Catholic Croats before Christmas in 1992 remained where they were until the religious festivities were over, until at least the 6th of January, 1993. What happened on the 4th of January, 1993, one of the attempts to take down the national symbol of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina resulted in this warning shot fired by a member of the military police of the HVO because that wasn't the first such incident at the time of these religious holidays.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to a different subject unless there are more questions from the -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I have a question. The intimation of the indictment is that someone from the HVO fired at the soldier who was taking down the flag. You say the soldier fired into the air, not in any way aiming at that soldier. Can you tell the Chamber on what you base this affirmation? Has there been an investigation and you have seen the result of it, or have you had a report on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if a member of the military police of the HVO had fired at someone taking down the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, if he had done that at the time he would have certainly killed him because he was only about ten metres away from him. But he fired in the air to frighten him and to warn him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Just to conclude this, and then I will move on. Were you present when this happened, this, you say, shooting in the air?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present, but I was told about this in very precise terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a follow-up question. I understand in Gornji Vakuf during the religious festivities one put up these flags; but as far as you know, was this done in Herzegovina, in areas where the Catholic Croats were present? Was this done in general terms or more precisely just in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this wasn't only something that was done in Gornji Vakuf. This was usually done to celebrate the religious festivities of the Croats throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did this cost -- did this custom have its roots in history, in the past? You are not perhaps an historian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did, Your Honours. My father would put up the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in his house because he couldn't do it outside at the time of the Communist regime, and everyone else acted in the same way. That's a tradition of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to clarify this problem, would you allow me to put a very brief question to the witness with regard to this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This is a problem. I have to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, as a rule you shouldn't; but as you rarely take the floor, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Witness, every week there are weddings for all the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs are concerned. Can you tell the Chamber, when you have columns of people celebrating such weddings passing through the area, do they display symbols of any kind? What kind of symbols? I'm referring to flags. What kind of flags? Is this common practice? Was this common practice in the former Yugoslavia, and is it practice or has it been common practice since the 1990s up until the present day? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, it was common practice before 1990. When you had wedding columns one would display flags, but I should point out that before 1990 when the Croats had a wedding they would inverse the position for the Croatian flag, although this wasn't possible -- it wasn't allowed. Why was it upside down? Well, because our national flag, the national flag of the Croatian people, starts with a red square and the Yugoslav -- or, rather, has a red field whereas the Yugoslav one had a blue field, so you would turn it around. So in spite of the fact that there was a star on it, it would look red, white, and blue. After the multi-party elections, it was allowed to display those national symbols; and then before religious festivities and when weddings were held and at every other festivals, the Croats would display their national symbols, the Croatian flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslims would display their own symbols. They would display them at their weddings, and the Serbs would do the same. There were no exceptions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not happy with your answer. I was asking you what sort of flags they display now today, not just then. I said from then up until the present day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1990, I said one could display one's national symbols at weddings, festivals, birthdays, any kind of festivity, religious festivities and other forms of festivities. One could display the symbols of one's nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Praljak, please sit down, because the Chamber allowed Mr. Coric to put his question exceptionally. We know that these flags were used during various ceremonies. The only specification - and Mr. Witness, you did not respond it to quite - the question is, is that what is happening today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you're on your feet for the question of flags or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not directly. I have nothing to ask the witness. I would just like to address Your Honours with two sentences. [In English] Yes, yes. [Interpretation] I insist that I address the Court in this connection with two sentences. Judge Trechsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this court has rules, and everyone has to conform to them. We have been normally quite lenient, but there are limits, and it is not possible at this time for any party to address the Court. This is not provided for. It's completely against the ruling, and we cannot make an exception for you unless we -- we lose our face by being completely inconsequential. I'm sorry. I ask you to accept this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can accept it, but on Monday, Your Honours, you promised that you would set a time when we would discuss these things. The question of flags is a technical issue. I wish to say that I sign every guild of the free man of Praljak an independent autonomous person in Bosnia-Herzegovina to hang up his flag whenever he wants. We are spending months here riding a question that has not been posed in France or Switzerland or America. I have my own flag, and I wish to sign any guild that ensues from this. What is the question we are discussing here? With the Croatian people a sovereign nation in a state, will they hoist their flags two days earlier or two days later, and then will anyone have the right to trample on it? We have been wasting a lot of time. There is no rule that would sanction such behaviour. That is my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Prosecutor raised the question of flags according in line with the indictment. Apparently, the witness has given us certain element and explained to us that this was a religious custom. There was no need for you to intervene, to add you personal opinion about the issue. It is an additional waste of time. There is the submission of the Prosecution, the witness responds, and you can have a witness brought in to testify about this if you wish to do so. There will be plenty of occasions to come back to this. And as my colleague has said, this is not the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a criminal court. What crime prohibits this? Somebody can say that I am walking, and you will question me whether I have the right to walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we have understood what you said. I'm telling you that this question of flags is now clear to everyone, and we will now move on to another subject. Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As promised, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I would like you to look at another document, Mr. Batinic. It's in the same binder. It's number P 01351. It's P 01351, and there should be a B/C/S version. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You can see that it's from the operative zone of North-west Herzegovina, the Prozor forward command post, and that it's dated 20-something January 1993. And from the last page we can see that it's signed by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, who was the commander of this operative zone. I take it you have not seen the document before, have you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Again, however, I'd like to ask you a few questions as to what is contained in the document and see if that complies or doesn't comply with your knowledge at the time. You can see that it is on the first page a report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf on the 28th of January, 1993, and that would have been the time when you were with the HVO. If you go to page 2 in the B/C/S version, you will see that there is a Roman number I, and it deals with Uzricje. And I apologise for my pronunciation. Have you found the section on Uzricje, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is in number 4 on that list of issues that Siljeg brings up regarding Uzricje, and it says there that a total of 24 houses destroyed (22 torched, 2 shelled), and goes on to number 5: "Looted two tractors and seven luxury cars." Were you aware of the HVO burning of houses and looting in Uzricje at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Is this something that was -- or the question of whether there were burning or looting, is this something that was discussed between the HVO soldiers where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time referred to in this document, I was in the so-called industrial zone, that is, in the factories together with a group of home guards, and we did not have information about this kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told -- excuse me, I'm told that on number 5 there may be a mistranslation. Perhaps the gentleman can read on number 5 where in English it says: "looted two tractors and seven luxury cars." What does it say actually in Croatian? And also, I haven't read the entire report, but on number 4 where it talks about the 24 houses having been destroyed, I don't see that this was actually done intentionally by the HVO as the question would appear, as it was posed by Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't help much on the translation issue, but maybe the interpreter could read out the B/C/S section on number 5 on Uzricje, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The witness can read. The interpreter or the translator can translate. That's why we have the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Witness, please, you see number 5 there. Could you please read that out in your language.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 5 of this document says: "Taken away: Two tractors and seven luxury cars."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Some of the same words are used for a different -- or regarding a different village, and since this is now a language issue, I'd like you to read out that, as well, and I'll direct you to it. Can you see under number 5, there's a Roman number II to Dusa.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And if you go down that list, you get finally to a number 4. That might very well be on your next page. And the number 4 in my English version, it says: "A total of 18 houses and sheds were destroyed," and it goes on. Could you please start reading in number 4 what it says.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 4, under the heading Dusa, it says: "Totally destroyed 18 houses and sheds, of which 16 were torched and 2 houses from the consequences of shelling."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Can you go on please and read number 5 as well. That comes after the section that you just read.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 5: "Driven away: Two tractors, two TAMs, and seven luxury cars."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try and phrase my questions more generally. First, did I understand you correctly that you said at this point, let's say the last part of January, you were in the industrial zone with the Home Guard, which is close to the town? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And in general, you didn't then know what was going on in the villages like Uzricje and Dusa. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: A general question, then. Were you aware of any intentional burning of Muslim houses or -- and/or any looting of Muslim property carried out by HVO members?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Unless there are any questions from the Chamber, I will move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, this is quite a different subject, and I'm now moving away from Gornji Vakuf again. You testified on direct examination by Mr. Karnavas regarding some meetings of the Central Board of the HDZ in February 1992, more specifically about Mr. Kljuic and his position at the time. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And do I understand you correctly that what you said was the following: "On the 2nd of February, 1992, during the meeting that was in Siroki Brijeg, Kljuic felt that he no longer had the support of most of the members of the Central Committee of the HDZ, and as a result, he resigned." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but the interpreter didn't say that to me. If I hadn't heard it from you, I couldn't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not quite sure what you're referring to. Could you say again, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was not fully interpreted by the interpreter service working for this Tribunal. I heard you when you asked whether that was correct, and I said, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So you heard me in English, in other words?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. You were aware, though, when it comes to Kljuic that there had been discussions about his role in the leadership of the HDZ BiH prior to this 2nd of February meeting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And you knew, didn't you, that Tudjman and Susak and Boban, that they were unhappy with Kljuic and that they wanted him out of the leadership of the HDZ BiH, and because of that pressure, he resigned. Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know what you were just saying, that Mr. Kljuic as president of the HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina was not desirable to Mr. Tudjman, Susak, and Boban. I really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you yet another document and quote from that and see if that -- if you can tell me and comment on that. Let's start with it. And that would be a document that is, again, in your binder, and it's number P 00134. Have you found that, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Yes. P 00134, and it starts with a page numbered 99. Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: For your information, that's a transcript from a meeting at the office of President Franjo Tudjman of Croatia, and it's from the 3rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: For counsel, this has priorly been admitted before. This is, then, from page 99.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And I'll read parts of it out to you, Mr. Batinic. If you go down and you see the president, his second entry, it starts with: "All right." And then it goes on three paragraphs down to: "Mate can inform us briefly." Then it goes on: "However" - this is President Tudjman speaking - "However, as you know events have unfolded in the BH HDZ in such a way that Stjepan Kljuic who, after the mistake with Perinovic, was excellent for that who managed the election campaign brilliantly, but afterwards, recently, partially" -- excuse me -- "practically disappeared under Alija Izetbegovic's fez and the HDZ practically stopped leading an independent Croatian policy, our policy. This went so far, but just as Alija said that the war in Croatia was not his war, so Stjepan Kljuic told foreign newspapers - I do not know whether he did it here, too - but people told me that he said that we had ourselves to blame for this situation for the war. In circumstances such as they were, with representatives from Western Herzegovina and the Croatian Bosnian Posavina coming to us over the last year and a half and us forming our policies together with them, he was evermore distant from these policies. "We, let me not repeat things, it is known what we said, what we told these people of ours who even wanted to take a decision when the Serbs practically separated, when Alija conducted such a policy, our people, people came with the proposal that a declaration be adopted on unification with Croatia. "I was the one who held them back, and we said no, because of the international situation, so that we would not be in an awkward situation." And I'll continue until the end of Mr. Tudjman's entry so you have it all. Tudjman continues: "We also told Kljuic to talk both to the Muslims and Izetbegovic and to the Serbs. However, he did not do this. He became increasingly distant from the part of the HDZ, which was ready to implement these policies, and he then practically came to his resignation. Now, I would like to get back on stage as his own way. Therefore, the way things are is that we should hold a session of the Main Board there, and instead of him who has resigned, we should elect a new president while the convention elections, et cetera, they will be held when the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is over. That is all from me. Thank you. Mate, the floor is yours." Mr. Batinic, what Tudjman basically says here is that Kljuic had to go, isn't it, because he's not willing to adopt an independent Croatian policy of the HDZ of Posavina and Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He can -- she can ask what Tudjman said. Now she's paraphrasing and interpreting what Tudjman supposedly had said. I don't read it that way. Now, if she reads it that way, that's her -- that's her problem, but the question should be posed: "Can you give us an explanation? Can you give us an opinion on this?" Keeping in mind the date, the date of when this occurred. Tudjman doesn't say anything about Kljuic being forced out. Kljuic resigned on his own. And in light of this question, perhaps the gentleman should be allowed to refer to his notebook when he was there during the meeting and took copious notes as to what exactly occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may. I'm asking a leading question as part of my cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas has provided us with his interpretation of what was said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, Madam Prosecution is presenting her case, and she's entitled to present her arguments as she wishes. Now, the witness may agree with her or not. She puts her question in the way she wishes. That is her job, and the witness can say I don't agree and explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree with you except for the fact that if she's going to quote from a document, she then can't misstate the facts of the document. She could ask -- she can point to the particular aspect of the document, the one sentence or two where Tudjman supposedly says that they fired Kljuic, if that's what she wants to put, but that's not the case. It's quite obvious for me something different, so if she wants to quote the particular passage and say, is this what Tudjman's saying, that's fine. But the way the question is being posed, she's mischaracterising the facts, and that's what I object to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I still believe I am entitled to ask the question, and it's then up to the witness who is the one testifying here to say whether he agrees or not or sees it differently. But before we get to that and since Mr. Karnavas raised the issue of the date, I am afraid I have misread the date. The right date, according to page 1 of the transcript that has already been admitted, is 10th of March, 1992. So it's 1992, not 1993. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of March, 1992, was 34 days following the resignation of the president of the HDZ for BiH, Mr. Kljuic as president. So this is 34 days after his resignation. So I cannot agree, Madam Prosecutor, for the simple reason that this document needs to be read out in its entirety, and in a part of this document it is stated that they had told Kljuic to talk to the Muslims and the Serbs and that he hadn't done that. And as a result, he didn't implement the policies expected of him, and then, naturally, members of the Central Board realised this at a meeting in Siroki Brijeg, and when Mr. Kljuic realised that he no longer enjoyed the support of those same people, it was only logical for him to resign.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll move on unless the Trial Chamber has questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, I'm still with the HDZ issue, so to speak, the HDZ politics, and I'd like again to go back to something you said during Mr. Karnavas's direct examination. And when it came to the status of the Croats in BiH, you said that it was important for the Croats to be a constituent people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that it was important for us. We are a constituent people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that's what you wanted to be also, say, back in 1991, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we are a constituent people, Madam Prosecutor. It wasn't necessary for us to want something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll ask you a different question, then -- or, actually, I'll refer back to a question asked by Mr. Karnavas. He asked you whether there is a distinction between being a constituent people and a minority. Can you remember that question? National minority. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an important distinction to be made between the term "a constituent people" and the term "a national minority," which you might have anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Batinic. I'd like to go back to what you said during direct examination by Mr. Karnavas, and I'd like you to listen and see if that's the correct quote, and that's on line -- sorry, page 54 from the first -- Monday transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: "A constituent nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, the constituent nations were the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, and they were in fact" -- and then there's a word missing, but it refers to that "they are the statehood of BiH." And am I understanding you correctly that that would be the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims that were to be the constituent peoples of BiH? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims -- well, it's not as if they were supposed to be or had to be the constituent peoples. From the time that Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded as a state, they were the constituent peoples in that state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to the distinction between national minority --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think it is very important. Otherwise, we will not go in not necessary question. I think -I'm not sure, I think - that I have heard that the witness said since foundation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So obviously, he's referring to the history, which is the case by the constitution before -- yeah. Now, the others are telling me that they also understand. But if that is clear, then it would not -- then it would not be further questions unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Well, my question referred to the status of a constituent people and the status of a national minority without any specific time references. This issue might take a little while, though, so if the Chamber wants to -- wants to break, we can do that. Otherwise, I'll go on. I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a break. We'll have our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During the break, Your Honour, if I may suggest that perhaps our colleague consult with Mr. Tomljanovich. His mentor who guided him at Yale to get his Ph.D., Ivo Banac, has written the probably the seminal book, the seminal book, on national minorities in the area. Perhaps that might assist my colleagues on that side in learning the distinction between what is a constituent nation and what is a national minority. It's a critical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I won't belabour it, but there's no reason for -- with great respect, I appreciate Mr. Karnavas's desire to be helpful. We know quite well. We've read a lot of this material. But the questions are put for a particular reason, and you have to give counsel a chance to conduct her examination, as Mr. Karnavas often says, step-by-step. It's not that we don't know. I certainly -- I think I know. I'm not a native of the former Yugoslavia, my apologies, but I've researched the situation quite extensively. I don't think we need to be lectured on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to a statement that you made on Monday, Mr. Batinic, and I'm going to give a transcript reference to Mr. Karnavas and counsel, but you won't have it in front of you, so I'm asking you to listen to me. It's page 34321, and the question is from line 1, and the question you were asked, Mr. Batinic is: "All right. Now, is there a distinction between being a constituent nation and a national minority and, if so, could you please tell us what that distinction is?" And your answer was: "As the constituent nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, the constituent nations were the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, and they were, in fact, the bearers of the statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as a constituent people, any one of those three peoples mentioned had the right to expect that they could participate in government, that government would be shared between the constituent peoples in an equal manner. National minorities could not expect or count on being included in this division of power, in sharing in government, and that's the significant distinction that has to be made." Can you remember making that statement, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: What do you mean by a constituent people having the right to expect that government would be shared between the constituent peoples in an equal manner? And I'm interested in what you mean by "shared in an equal manner."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A constituent people has the right to expect to be represented in government, in a government of which they are a state-forming factor. They will be on an equal footing with other constituent peoples. National minorities have all civil rights and other forms of rights. They can participate in government, but this is not necessary, whereas representatives of constituent peoples do have to participate in governmental bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And what do you mean by saying "on equal footing with other constituent peoples"? Maybe you can give an example.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the constituent peoples has the right and rightly expects to be represented in an equal manner at all levels of power in the state in question, in the state referred to. To have equal rights means that this concerns the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims -- or, rather, in this particular case, the Bosniaks as they're called today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'm still asking you what you mean by "equal manner," "equal footing." Does it mean, for example, for one Croat in government, one Muslim in government?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is quite correct. So it is an issue of parity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to have a look at another document that was brought up during Mr. Karnavas's cross -- excuse me, direct examination, and that would be in the binder you have in front of you, and it's number 1D 02700. That should be the Statute of the HDZ BiH from 1993. Oh, sorry, it was in the -- in the second binder. Thank you. Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at one of the articles that were showed you by Mr. Karnavas yesterday -- excuse me, the day before, and that's Article 10, number 1, 10.1, and it should be on page 3 in your document in B/C/S. Have you found Article 10.1?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: In Article 10.1 and I'm going to read it out to you, it says the following: "To ensure the right of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina to self-determination and" -- excuse me: "...to self-determination and statehood, independence and sovereignty, in the sovereign, independent and internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisting of three equal constitutive nations (Croats, Muslims, and Serbs), and has the internal political structure of a state consisting of three constitutive units." Am I correct in understanding that this Article 10.1, it means that there would be three nations in three different constitutive units, so three units within BiH, one Croat, one Serb, and one Muslim unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partially right. In 10.1, the HDZ Bosnia-Herzegovina states its support for a Bosnia and Herzegovina, the internal structure of which would include constituent units representing three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Each constituent unit would have its people in some kind of a majority, and within, let's say, the framework of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina or a union of the republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, relationships would be determined between these three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Right. So if I'm understanding you correctly, you're saying that there are three -- or what it refers to in Article 10.1 is three constitutive units, and in one of those units the Serbs would be in minority -- excuse me, majority; in the second unit, the Croats would be in majority; and in the third unit, the Muslims would be in majority?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And in the Croat unit, then, would the Muslims then be a constituent people with the right to participate in the government of that unit on an equal footing with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any constituent unit, anyone from one of the three constituent peoples would have a constituent status. So a Croat in a unit where the Muslims were in a majority, a Croat in a unit where the Serbs were in a majority, and vice versa, Serbs and Muslims in a constituent unit where the Croats were in the majority. You can't take away the right of being a constituent people from any of the three constituent peoples in any square metre of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So are you, then, saying that in the constituent unit where the Croats would be a majority, there would be one Muslim for one Croat in government, so one Muslim for one Croat in government in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship would be agreed on on the basis of reciprocity between the federal units within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But are you -- does that mean that in the constituent unit where the Croats would be a majority there would be one Muslim for one Croat in government? That was my question, and I don't think you've answered it specifically.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't briefly answer your question. I said that this relationship within the federal units was -- well, if it had been established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would have been established on the basis of reciprocity between the three constituent peoples. At the level of the state, naturally, that relationship would be a relationship based on parity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you are saying is interesting. I'm trying to follow you because the subject is extremely complicated. If we take the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, if I have understood what you have said correctly, in this case the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims at the level of state would be on an equal footing. That is to say there would be, for example, a Presidency of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. There would be a Serbian deputy, a Muslim deputy, and a Croatian deputy, and these three would rotate, be president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Is that in fact what you are actually saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. When I mentioned the state level, well, at the level of the state there would be a relationship of parity, and in that case I was thinking of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the governmental bodies, because only the state can carry out certain joint activities. Within constituent units where the Croats were in the majority, Serbs or Muslims, the government would be established on reciprocity agreed on by the parties, or if this had been the case, by representatives of federal units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm making a hypothesis. Let's imagine that the Republic of Herceg-Bosna has been recognised by everyone. What would have happened on the political level in your opinion? Would there have been this notion of constituent people? Would this notion have been maintained within the Republic of Herceg-Bosna and, if so, does this mean that there would automatically be in all spheres of authority a Serb, a Croat, and a Muslim, or is this -- would this be another system? It's a hypothesis that I'm putting forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can answer this in the following way: No one ever asked representatives of the HDZ for an independent Republic of Herceg-Bosna. As a political party which had the full support of the Croatian people, we supported an internal structure base on the federal model. The Republic of Herceg-Bosna wouldn't be internationally recognised, only the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised within a federation between three republics. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the federal level, how would power have been shared in the Republic of Herceg-Bosna within the framework of this federal state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? How would power have been exercised at the level of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the three federal units would have had to have its own constitution, its own government. It couldn't have had its own currency or relationships with other states as a sovereign and independent state, so such activities would have to be transferred to state authorities in which Serbs, Croats, and Muslims would participate on an equal footing. Within one constituent unit, one assumed that power would be organised on the basis of reciprocity, as I said, on the basis of reciprocity of federal units in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, there would be representation of people who weren't in the majority, which was in proportion to the number of the inhabitants of the second or third people in that constituent unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must confess, Mr. Batinic, that I'm not quite clear yet what -- what your answer is; and second, I'm not clear on what you base it. If I -- if I take the essence, the unit, as in Croat, Serb, would be a Croat, Serb, Muslim unit in the first place; and on the other side, the other ethnicities within that unit would nevertheless have a function of a constituent nation, but their representation in government would be a matter of reciprocity. Now, I could imagine that reciprocity means if you Muslims in your unit put a portion of Croats in your government, we Croats in Herceg-Bosna will put an adequate portion of Muslims in our government. I'm not complicating it by including the Serbs, but of course, that's only for economy. Is that what you mean by reciprocity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then I have this other question: On what basis do you affirm this? Which document contains a sketch of this -- of this solution or even maybe an elaborate -- an elaborate plan or concept or programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no such document. This was just drafted as a proposal for policies that the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina would support at a time that this statute was created in 1993, on the 17th of December. So these questions were questions that had to be agreed on with the other two constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was this plan, this draft, was this put on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as far as I know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So it is your point that we just take your word for it, that this was discussed and that there was a general agreement on this. Is that finally the basis of what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the political tendencies that the HDZ expressed with regard to the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Following these proposals, the representatives of the Croatian people accepted certain plans that were to come into force in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the insistence of the international community. I have the Vance-Owen Plan in mind above all and everything else that happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will leave it at that for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have a few more questions on this, Mr. Batinic. So if I understand you correctly, you say that representation in government within the Croat unit would be decided on reciprocity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the remaining two federal units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But I'm talking within the Croat unit, though. Are you saying that representation by the Serbs and the Muslims in government within the Croat unit would be decided on reciprocity with the two other units of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But what do you mean by reciprocity? And that's within the unit I'm still referring to.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have at the level of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina a parity government formed through which at every inch of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory the equality and equal rights of all three nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina are ensured, then when it comes to the formation of government in the constituent units, the participation of the nation that is not the majority in one of the three would be reciprocal and in proportion to their numbers and agreed upon among the three units. I'm not a legal expert, especially not an expert on constitutional law, but I know what we basically had in mind in the statute and other documents of the HDZ and in our programme declarations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: But did you within the Croat unit, again, did you have in mind that the Muslims would be a constituent people or a national minority?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. This has been asked, and it's been answered repeatedly. The gentleman has said that they would be constituent as they were throughout every single inch. Now, I don't understand what part they don't get. I would also ask the Trial Chamber to recall that we heard a lot of testimony about the Cutileiro Plan, which answered all the questions that were being posed by the Bench. And also, we have another plan, which is the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, which is exactly what the gentleman is saying even though he's not being given an opportunity to look at those documents, because it's -- it's exactly what he's saying. But I don't understand. Why is it that over and over again we're trying to suggest that the Croats are trying to disenfranchise one of the nations when that is not the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, the witness has already answered your question that you're asking regarding the question of minorities and constituent peoples. He was quite clear about it. So going back to it is immediately provoking an intervention by Mr. Karnavas, as we have had other witnesses and high-level jurists discussing these constitutional issues. The witness has just told us that he's not a legal expert, so it's better to move on to another subject unless in view of the position that he had in this municipality of Gornji Vakuf he might on the political level be able to answer certain questions but not the legal issues of a minority and a constituent people. We have spent maybe hundreds of hours discussing this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll take that on board, Your Honour, and I'll -- Mr. President, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Batinic, you said that from, I think, January 1993 there were basically two separate municipal administrations in Gornji Vakuf, a Muslim and a Croat one. Is that the correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in January, but when the conflict ceased in January and February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Okay. And to move forward a few words, there were municipal elections in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And after the 1997 elections, was there to be set up a joint administration in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. This is outside the scope of the indictment. I object on relevance. If we could hear what the relevance is, perhaps, then the Trial Chamber may be able to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may have some relevance. Please explain, madam. What is the relevance of this question, of addressing the elections of 1997?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Well, firstly, if Mr. Karnavas's objection goes to me getting into post-Dayton issues, I'd like to refer to Mr. Karnavas's direct examination where he touched upon the 1997 statute of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That was an exhibit that was tendered. And Mr. Batinic, also, in his testimony touched upon the issue of the name of the municipality, Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje. That was, I think, brought up when Mr. Praljak did his cross-examination, but I might be mistaken there. The document that I'm about to go into does refer to the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, what happened there, and it deals with Mr. Batinic directly. Also, I'd like to point out that this, in the Prosecution's opinion, goes to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First and foremost, the 1997 document that was shown was -- shows that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is still in existence, and it's registered legally, and it showed the coat of arms. That's first of all. It has nothing to do with any elections in that particular municipality. So that's a red herring to suggest that somehow the door has been opened with that. With respect to the name, I don't -- I don't see where in the indictment there's anything making reference that the use of the Croatian historical name of that area, Uskoplje, is somehow tied into the indictment, so another that's red herring. They're actually -- they're suggesting that it goes to the gentleman's credibility. Perhaps we need to hear a little bit more. How is it it goes -- these elections in 1997 go to the gentleman's credibility as to what he saw, what he heard, you know, and what he did during the relevant period of the indictment in that particular area, and we're talking 1991, 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, regarding credibility, it's on the basis of the credibility of the witness that you wish to address the elections of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Well, these are not exactly the elections in 1997. It's something that happened in Gornji Vakuf subsequent to the elections of 1997 that involves Mr. Batinic. That's my first point. My second point is that I still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My second point is that -- or did the President mean for me to go ahead? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Batinic, we had established, I believe, that there were municipal elections in 1997 and that you were to set up a joint administration in Gornji Vakuf. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And were you involved with the HDZ or with the municipality authorities, the municipal authorities in Gornji Vakuf at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the Municipal Board of HDZ for the municipality of Uskoplje at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Did you have any position within the municipality authorities? Were you head of department of finance?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997, I was head of the municipality of Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific? Does that mean president of the Executive Committee, something similar to what you were before the war, or is it something else you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to an administrative arrangement for the Croatian people. I'm talking about the municipality of Uskoplje, and I was "nacelnik" or head of the Uskoplje municipality in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And were you involved in these efforts to set up a joint administration in the municipality subsequent to the 1997 elections?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Is it true that you were banned from municipal political activities in 1998 by the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And is that, to put it in simple terms, and I'll go into the document, but would that be because the local bodies of Gornji Vakuf didn't manage to form a joint administration, which was required by the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were appointed, but they didn't start functioning jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document. You might have it in front of you already. It's 1D 02789. It's probably in the binder that you have in front of you. Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: We see it's from the election appeals subcommission from the OSCE mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's dated 20th of July, 1998. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Is this the decision that bans you from political activities, to put it simply, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this decision, political activity was not prohibited to me, but what I was not allowed to do was to take part in the bodies of authority in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to read out very few sections of this document and see if they comply with your understanding. And on the first page here, on page 1, it says: "Decision of the Judges." And it says: "With regard to the appeal lodged by the head of the OSCE mission relating to non-observance of conditions laid down by the arbitration decision on results of the municipal elections in Gornji Vakuf municipality in 1997." So that was the basis, wasn't it, the non-compliance with an arbitration decision? You touched upon it already, but this is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And I'd like you, then, to go to page 9 of the B/C/S version that you have in front of you. It should be on page 12 of the English version. Have you found it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Do you see the second whole paragraph? It starts with "The sanctions in this case." On page 9. Do you have that? It's the last full paragraph on page 9, I believe. It should be on your screen as well. Do you have it? Maybe it's -- it should be on your screen. It starts with "The sanctions." Do you have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Could the usher please be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So what it -- what it says is the following: "The sanctions in this case were imposed on the basis of the results of the Electoral Appeals Subcommission investigation. The Electoral Appeals Subcommission finds that the HDZ is continuing to link the matter of changing the name of the municipality with the implementation of the electoral results in Gornji Vakuf municipality in contravention of the arbitration decision." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written down corresponds to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And when it refers to the matter of changing the name, that's the question of changing the name from Gornji Vakuf to Uskoplje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is the request of the Croats of Uskoplje for the municipality to be called Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: This decision, is it correct that that referred to you personally but also to an Abdulah Topcic representing the coalition, including the SDA, as well as the HDZ as that political body?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Before we leave the document, I'll just like to look at the decision itself so you can confirm that. That should be on page 15 in the English version and on page 12 in the B/C/S version. Do you have it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So it says here "Decision," and it says: "First - On the grounds of its powers to determine condign penalties, the Electoral Appeals Subcommission hereby orders that Zdravko Batinic, son of Lafko [phoen], be immediately relieved of the post of chief of the department of the economy and finance ..." I'll just stop there for a second. Is that a position that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a position that I should have had in the joint administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll go on. " ... and be replaced by an individual to be nominated by the HDZ in accordance with the procedure of appointments to executive posts. Furthermore, the Electoral Appeals Subcommission orders that Batinic be prohibited from occupying any other executive position in the municipal bodies of the authorities in Gornji Vakuf, including an official or an unofficial position, and from attending any meetings of the Municipal Council or other sessions in the municipal government of Gornji Vakuf." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're reading out what is written there. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If you go to the second -- what is marked "Second "right below this, that's the dismissal of Topcic of the coalition, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then in the third one, it says: "The Electoral Appeals Subcommission reprimands the HDZ and the coalition for unprofessional conduct, which prevents Gornji Vakuf Municipal Council from carrying out its legislative duties." That's correct, as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Just very quickly to another document on the same issue and then -- because I can see the clock ticking towards quarter to 2.00. Could you please look up the document that is very close to this one in your binder, I believe. It's 1D 02792. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: We can see it's another document from the Election Appeals Subcommission of the OSCE, and it's dated a little less than a month later. You can see up in the left-hand corner, it's dated 25th of August, 1998. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: At this time in August 1998, were you running for the -- or were you going to run for the HDZ in the elections?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the list of candidates of the HDZ for the general elections in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If we could go to -- I believe it's the last page or page 3 in B/C/S. It's page 4 in the English version, and it's a fairly long paragraph. It's the only full paragraph that you should have on your page, and around the middle of that, it says the following: "Had the Election Appeals Subcommission known of Batinic's candidacy, it would have removed him from the HDZ list of candidates. However, the election appeals subcommission now..." so this is August 1998, "... has new and material evidence of his current candidacy. The Election Appeals Subcommission finds that because of his previous actions, Batinic is barred from running in the 1998 elections, as his conduct violated the rules and regulations of the provisional appeals commission as described in detail in the first decision of 20th of July, 1998. Consequently, the Election Appeals Subcommission finds that Batinic is not qualified to run as a candidate of the HDZ party in the cantonal Assembly elections in Canton 6 (the Central Bosnia canton)." And by this, you were barred from running -- or from being a candidate of the HDZ in these elections. Is that correct, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Me and some 20 or so of my colleagues on the HDZ lists were also removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And these colleagues, had they been banned from certain activities as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a similar decision, they were removed from the list of candidates of the HDZ for the general elections in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And they were removed by the OSCE like you were?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO BATINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, contrary to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitution of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitution of the canton of Central Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, we're going to stop there now because it's time, and as there is a hearing later on, we shouldn't create problems for the Judges who will come after us. We will resume work tomorrow at 9.00, and the Chamber will render its oral decision regarding the request for additional time. The Prosecution has used 2 hours, 23 [as interpreted] minutes, so you have another 1 hour and 32 minutes left. 1 hour, 32 minutes. Witness, you will come back here tomorrow for the continuation of the cross-examination. There's an error in the transcript. The Prosecution has used 2 hours, 28 minutes, not 23, 28 minutes. I usually don't make errors in subtracting numbers. So you have 1 hour, 32 minutes left. Witness, I wish you and everyone else in the courtroom a good afternoon, and we'll meet again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
